title: The Album That Nearly Changed Everything — Adnan Sami Was Making Music With Michael Jackson Before the World Lost Him
excerpt: The Padma Shri singer just revealed he had three songs finalized with the King of Pop for a Motown-meets-Indian-music album. Then 2009 happened.
body:
Adnan Sami grew up listening to the Jacksons. Every bass line he ever wrote, he says, traces back to something he absorbed from their music as a kid. So when Jermaine Jackson called him — and Adnan's family told the actual Jermaine Jackson that Adnan was sleeping and could he please call back — the irony was not lost on anyone.

"My family said, 'Kisi Jackson ka call aaya tha,'" Adnan told Radio Nasha in a newly aired interview that has set Indian music circles buzzing. "Later, my manager also told me Jermaine had tried to reach me. I remember thinking how they might have felt — that I was playing hard to get."

He was not playing hard to get. He was, in fact, about to enter one of the most extraordinary chapters of his career — a chapter that ended before it could be written.

## How an Afghan Wife in Chandigarh Changed Music History

The connection began with Jermaine Jackson's wife, Halima Rashid, who is of Afghan origin and lived in Chandigarh for a period. She discovered Adnan's music while in India — the soaring vocals, the relentless bass guitar work, the way he could make a piano sound like it was confessing something — and carried his albums back to Los Angeles.

Jermaine listened. Then he played them for Michael. Then he played them for Janet.

"The most amazing part was that I grew up in awe of Michael Jackson and The Jacksons," Adnan recalled, "and he told me he really liked how I used the bass guitar. I was overwhelmed and told him that I learnt all of it from him."

The plan was ambitious. Michael Jackson, fresh from being cleared of all allegations against him, wanted to stage a comeback — but not solo. The first step would be a reunion album with The Jacksons, and they wanted it to sound like nothing the family had ever made before. A world music format. Motown meets Indian classical. Bass lines alongside the sarangi. Tabla-dholak patterns woven into pop arrangements.

And they wanted Adnan Sami to produce it.

## Three Songs, Two Years, One Phone Call Away

Adnan flew to Los Angeles three times. He and Michael spoke regularly on the phone. They finalised three songs based on Adnan's original compositions. The collaboration was to be his first English-language album — produced by the Jacksons, with Adnan singing on at least one track.

"It was progressing slowly," Adnan said in an earlier interview with Bollywood Hungama. "They like to work at their own pace. No hurry." He described the Jacksons as "very humble people — always attentive to what I say, always open to innovations and suggestions."

Nearly two years of work had gone into the project. Three songs were locked. The fusion was taking shape — something genuinely unprecedented, the first full-fledged collaboration between an Asian musician and one of America's greatest musical dynasties.

Then, on June 25, 2009, Michael Jackson died.

"Unfortunately, Michael passed away, and with that, the album also ended," Adnan said. The emotion in his voice, even years later, is unmistakable.

## What Survived — and What's Coming

The collaboration didn't disappear entirely. Jermaine Jackson reached out to Adnan afterward: "He told me that we had worked so hard together, so why not continue and do something together anyway?" The two went on to produce a song together — "Let's Go To Mumbai City" — a track that blended Motown grooves with a love letter to the city.

More recently, Adnan confirmed he is producing a full comeback album for the Jackson siblings, with **Janet Jackson** stepping in to fill Michael's role alongside Jermaine, Tito, Randy, Jackie, and Marlon. "Janet will bring her unique style to the songs," Adnan said. "It will be a different kind of collaboration — something nobody has seen before."

The album promises the same Motown-meets-Bollywood fusion that was originally conceived with Michael. A tribute, a continuation, and possibly the closest the world will ever get to hearing what that lost album might have sounded like.

## Why This Story Matters to the Diaspora

Adnan Sami's career arc is itself a diaspora story. Born in London to a Pakistani diplomat father and raised across the subcontinent, he chose Indian citizenship in 2016 — a decision that made headlines and drew both praise and controversy. He received the Padma Shri in 2020.

For NRIs who grew up on both "Lift Karade" and "Thriller," the idea that these two musical worlds nearly collided in a recording studio is both thrilling and heartbreaking. It would have been the kind of crossover that doesn't just chart — it shifts how the world hears Indian musicians.

The Jackson-Sami album that never was remains one of Indian music's great what-ifs. But with the new project featuring Janet Jackson now in development, the story might not be over. Sometimes the music just takes longer to arrive than planned.

*Adnan Sami's latest single "Lipstick" is now streaming on all major platforms. The Jackson siblings album is currently in production.*
